newsitem.title: UK: Investors eye index-linked gilts as UK election nears.
newsitem.headline: Investors eye index-linked gilts as UK election nears.

text.p: Britain's index-linked government bonds, always a refuge from inflationary uncertainty, are now likely to be even more attractive as the political temperature rises ahead of the general election, analysts said on Thursday.

With the political conference season in full swing, a budget to follow in November and elections to be held by May 1997, the next few months could see investors head for inflation-proof gilts in droves.
"The index-linked market is set for a rally...and will increasingly be viewed as something of a safe haven," said Don Smith, economist at HSBC Markets.

Analysts said the party political conference season -- the opposition Labour Party is meeting this week, the ruling Conservatives next week -- always throws up some political bombs for the gilt market to defuse.

This year, a key worry for investors is that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke could cut interest rates and/or taxes overzealously in an attempt to fire the economy and boost flagging Conservative chances of re-election.
Index-linked gilts offer insurance against a possible inflationary effect of such moves.
"Some investors are worried that Clarke will follow policies not totally aimed at meeting the Maastricht targets," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.
"That would threaten the inflationary outlook in 1997," he said, adding that investors had been "nibbling" at index-linked gilts as a result.
The conventional gilt market has also been hurt by the refusal by both Britain's major political parties to commit to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Already, gilts have seen bond markets in countries pledged to join EMU shooting past in the fast lane. Swedish 10-year bonds are trading about 30 basis points through gilts and even the Spanish market is neck-and-neck.
Aside from the risks posed by a prolonged political battle in the run-up to elections, there are other inflationary alarm bells ringing.

Smith said inflation uncertainties had been stoked by August's inflation numbers, which saw underlying retail price inflation stick stubbornly at 2.8 percent year-on-year for the fourth month in a row.
He also noted a recent spike up in oil prices. "After taking account of likely petrol price rises...we have revised up our inflation profile."

He forecast underlying inflation at 3.0 percent in October but dropping thereafter. Other analysts are more pessimistic, predicting greater price pressures to come as British consumers spend furiously and the manufacturing economy recovers.

On top of inflation worries, whether politically inspired or not, the giddy heights reached by the British stock market in the shape of the FTSE-100 index of leading shares is viewed with suspicion by some investors and could also prompt some switching into index-linked gilts.
The FTSE pushed to a record high of 4,015 on Wednesday, clearing the magic 4,000 level for the first time.
In its latest monthly survey of fund managers' investment intentions, Merrill Lynch found UK institutional investors were increasingly pessimistic about equity markets worldwide.
The survey found British funds are increasing exposure to index-linked gilts and 80 percent of respondents expect UK inflation and interest rates to rise over the next year.
"Some investors are feeling a little nervous of the lofty value the stock market has reached and are viewing index-linked gilts as better relative value," Lewis said.
The supply side of the equation also favours index-linked stock, analysts said. Smith said the Bank of England was well-ahead of its index-linked funding schedule.
"With six months of the financial year gone...the authorities have already sold 75 percent of their index-linked funding requirement."
The Bank of England is expected to have to sell about 40 billion stg of gilts in 1996/97. It is committed to make 15 percent of that total index-linked.
